stem: A one-year-old boy is referred to your clinic due to an empty scrotum. On examination the left is in the scrotum and the right is in the inguinal canal. What the best recommendation to his parents?
srcNote: ? (uncertain in source) Other source key (Final 437 A Q21): One-year-old boy with bilateral palpable undescended testes. Relevant choices: A. Orchidopexy at one year of age B. Orchidopexy on an urgent basis Ans. A&B were considered correct
expl: A testis still in the inguinal canal at one year will not descend on its own (spontaneous descent stops after ~6 months) → orchidopexy now; the recommended window (6–12 months) has already arrived.

why.A: Correct.
why.B: Further waiting gains nothing after 6 months and adds fertility/malignancy risk.
why.C: Far too late — puberty repair worsens fertility and cancer risk.
why.D: A true UDT needs surgery, not reassurance.

stem: A mother brings her 6-year-old son to the clinic because she noticed that one of his testicles is sometimes not present in the scrotum. During the physical examination, the doctor observes that the testis can be easily brought down into the scrotum, but it moves back up shortly after. What is the most likely diagnosis?
srcNote: Source note (Final 441 F Q13): Original recall comment: ( not same scenario but same idea)
expl: A testis that can be brought down into the scrotum easily but rises again is a retractile testis (active cremasteric reflex) — normal, needs follow-up only.

why.A: A true UDT cannot be manipulated down into the scrotum.
why.B: Torsion is acutely painful, with a high-riding, tender testis.
why.D: An ectopic testis lies off the line of descent (perineum, thigh) and can't be brought into the scrotum.
why.E: A hernia is a groin/scrotal swelling, not an intermittently empty scrotum.

stem: A 2 months old girl was brought to the clinic with a history of left groin swelling that increases while crying and decreases during sleep. On physical examination, there is a reducible left inguinal swelling. Which ONE of the following is the appropriate management?
expl: Inguinal hernias in infants don't resolve and have a high risk of incarceration → herniotomy as early as possible (elective, soon after diagnosis).

why.A: Correct.

stem: A 2 year old boy has a right inguinal hernia came with his parents because it became irreducible for the last 6 hours with no skin changes. Which one of the following is the diagnosis?
srcNote: (Abdominal wall and herniae)
expl: A known hernia that becomes irreducible for 6 hours without skin changes = incarcerated inguinal hernia.

why.A: A hydrocele isn't "irreducible hernia" and transilluminates.
why.C: Lipoma isn't a hernia that became irreducible.
why.D: Strangulation would show skin changes, tenderness, systemic signs.

stem: A 5-year-old girl is referred your clinic with an umbilical swelling since birth. On physical examination the swelling is easily reducible, and a one-centimeter defect is felt at the umbilicus. What is the best advice to her parents?
srcNote: (Abdominal wall and herniae)
expl: Most umbilical hernias close by age 4–5; a persisting defect in a 5-year-old is unlikely to close → surgical repair.

why.A: Correct.
why.B: She is beyond the age of spontaneous closure.
why.D: No reason to wait to puberty.

stem: Child with undescended left testis. On palpation, a mass is felt in the left groin. Best radiological image to obtain pre-op?

opts.t: No further radiological imaging is needed

srcNote: (Common pediatric surgical problems)
expl: A palpable undescended testis is localized clinically — no imaging is needed before orchidopexy. Imaging also can't replace laparoscopy when the testis is impalpable.

why.A: Radiation for no benefit.
why.B: Not needed — the testis is palpable.
why.D: US adds nothing when the testis is already felt in the groin.

stem: What defect can cause an indirect inguinal hernia in children?
srcNote: Blank choices are shown exactly as missing in the source.
expl: Paediatric indirect hernias come from a patent processus vaginalis (congenital).

why.A: Correct.
why.B: Hesselbach's weakness = direct hernia in adults.

stem: A 5 month old baby girl presents with umbilical swelling. On examination, it is easily reducible. What is the management of this case?

opts.t: Surgical repair after age of 1 year if not spontaneously resolved
Surgical repair between 4-5 years of age if not spontaneously resolved

srcNote: Other source key (Final 438 F Q15): D. Surgical at 4 years of age if not spontaneously resolved D Other source key (Final 436 A Q22): D. Surgical repair between 3-4 years of age if not spontaneously resolved D Other source key (Final 435 F Q11 (p. 144)): D. Reassure and follow up Ans: D
expl: Infantile umbilical hernias usually close spontaneously → observe; repair at 4–5 years if persisting (earlier if very large or symptomatic).

why.A: Follow-up is needed in case it persists.

stem: A 6-month old boy was noticed by his mother to have bilateral scrotal swellings. Your exam revealed bilateral non-communicating scrotal hydroceles. What is the most appropriate management?

opts.t: Groin US to rule out hernia
Hydrocelectomy at age of 1-2 years if not resolved

expl: Infant hydroceles (small PPV, immature absorption) usually resolve by 6–12 months, up to 2 years → observe; operate (hydrocelectomy via a groin approach, ligating the PPV) at 1–2 years only if still present.

why.A: Too early — most resolve on their own.
why.B: Not needed — clinical exam (get above it, transillumination) distinguishes it.
why.C: Aspiration in children risks infection and recurrence (the PPV stays open).

stem: A one-year-old healthy girl presents to the emergency department with difficulty in defecation and occasionally passing streaks of blood with stool for 2 weeks. On the physical examination everything was normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
srcNote: (Lower GI bleeding)
expl: Painless streaks of blood with a normal anal examination in a toddler → juvenile polyp, the commonest cause of painless rectal bleeding at this age.

why.A: A fissure would be seen on examination (posterior midline tear) and causes pain on defecation.
why.C: An abscess is a visible, tender, red swelling.
why.D: Hirschsprung presents with delayed meconium, chronic constipation and distension, not rectal bleeding.

stem: A 3 month old had hernia and the father had a history of hernia treated by mesh and he wanted his child to be treated with a mesh also. What would you advice him?

opts.t: Mesh isn’t required as the child needs herniotomy only
Mesh is only for umbilical hernia

srcNote: (Abdominal wall and herniae) Blank choices are shown exactly as missing in the source.
expl: Paediatric inguinal hernia is a patent processus vaginalis — herniotomy (high ligation of the sac) is curative; the posterior wall is normal, so no mesh is needed.

why.A: Correct.
why.B: Not an absolute contraindication — just unnecessary.

stem: A newborn baby had a small raised red lesion on the nose, it started to appear slowly after 2 months of birth. What is the most likely lesion?
srcNote: ? The source marks its answer as uncertain; the original key is retained. Blank choices are shown exactly as missing in the source.
expl: A raised red lesion that appears in the first weeks after birth and grows slowly = infantile haemangioma (proliferates in the first year, then involutes).

why.A: AV malformations are usually present at birth and are fast-flow.
why.C: A port-wine stain is flat and present at birth.

stem: A 6-month old boy was noticed by his mother to have bilateral scrotal swellings. On examination you can get above the swelling and the transillumination test was positive. What's the cause of this condition?
srcNote: (hernia) Blank choices are shown exactly as missing in the source.
expl: In an infant, a scrotal swelling you can get above that transilluminates is a hydrocele, caused by a narrow patent processus vaginalis letting peritoneal fluid into the scrotum.

why.A: Lymphatic obstruction causes adult/secondary hydroceles, not the infant type.

stem: Mother complaining that her 1 year old boy scrotum is containing only one testis, when you examine the child the right testis is in the scrotum and the left testis is in the inguinal region and you can’t pull it down, what is the most likely diagnosis?
srcNote: (Common pediatric surgical problems)
expl: A testis lying in the inguinal region that cannot be pulled down into the scrotum is undescended.

why.A: A retractile testis can be brought down into the scrotum.
why.D: A hernia is a groin swelling with a cough impulse; the testis itself is the mass here.

stem: A 15-year-old boy presented with a history of left scrotal swelling associated with dragging sensation pain which increase with activity and reduced on supine position. The swelling is disappearing on supine position and increase in standing with negative transillumination test and you can get above it. What is the most likely diagnosis?
srcNote: (Common pediatric surgical problems)
expl: Adolescent, left side, dragging ache worse on activity, disappears lying down, does not transilluminate and you can get above it = varicocele (dilated pampiniform plexus).

why.A: You can't get above an inguinal hernia.
why.B: A haematocele follows trauma and doesn't disappear lying down.

stem: Picture of hypospadias of a 3-month-old baby, his parents brought him for circumcision. What is the best thing to do next?
srcNote: (Common pediatric surgical problems) The source refers to a picture, but no associated image is supplied.
expl: Hypospadias is a contraindication to circumcision — the foreskin is needed for the repair. Defer circumcision and re-evaluate (refer for hypospadias repair, usually 6–18 months).

why.A: Correct.
why.B: Circumcision would destroy tissue needed for the repair.
why.C: Isolated hypospadias doesn't need renal imaging.
why.D: Circumcision shouldn't be done at all until the hypospadias is repaired.

stem: A 12-year-old girl presented with a neck mass that moves a little bit with swallowing and protrusion of the tongue. What is the name of the surgical procedure to remove this pathology?
srcNote: (thyroid gland)
expl: Midline neck mass in a child moving with swallowing and tongue protrusion = thyroglossal duct cyst → Sistrunk operation (cyst + tract + central hyoid) to prevent recurrence.

why.A: Correct.

stem: 24 years old male presented with painful scrotal swelling for 1 month, no hx of trauma or cryptorchidism, on examination the right testicle is swollen and tense. The left testis is normal. What is next initial step in the management?
srcNote: (Common pediatric surgical problems) Source note (Final 436 A Q7): Answer: B (Common pediatric surgical problems) The answer was confirmed when Q was reviewed with the course organiser. workup for testicular cancer
expl: An adult with a tense, swollen, painful testis for a month needs scrotal ultrasound first — to separate a hydrocele from a testicular tumour or epididymo-orchitis — before any treatment.

why.A: Never aspirate before excluding a tumour.
why.C: Antibiotics before a diagnosis could miss a tumour.
why.D: Surgery comes after the diagnosis is confirmed.

stem: A 3 month old male infant presented to the pediatric surgery clinic with absence of right testis since birth. On examination the right testis was palpable in the right inguinal region and the left testis was located normally in the left hemiscrotum. What is the best time for doing right orchidopexy in this patient?
srcNote: (Common pediatric surgical problems) Other source key (Final 436 B Q4): Three-week-old boy with a palpable undescended testis: B. Observation till age of 1 year then orchidopexy if no descent Ans. B
expl: A palpable UDT is observed until 6 months (spontaneous descent still possible) and then corrected — orchidopexy between 6 and 12 months (Dr. Altokhais: ~6–9 months).

why.A: Too early — it may still descend.
why.D: Delay worsens fertility and malignancy risk.

stem: A 4-year-old boy is noted to have swelling in his right groin. He has no other symptoms. Physical examination shows no swelling, and both testes are in the scrotum, but the right spermatic cord is thickened with a positive cough impulse. What is the diagnostic imaging modality of choice to confirm the diagnosis?
srcNote: (Common pediatric surgical problems)
expl: A thickened cord with a cough impulse in a boy = clinical inguinal hernia ("silk sign") — no imaging needed.

why.A: CT isn't needed.
why.B: US only if the diagnosis is doubtful.

stem: A 6-year-old male presents with a left groin lump. On examination, cough impulse is positive and the lump is reducible and extends into the scrotum. The internal ring occlusion test is positive. What type of hernia does the patient have?
srcNote: (Abdominal wall and herniae)
expl: Reducible lump extending into the scrotum, controlled by occluding the deep ring = indirect inguinal hernia (via the deep ring); in a child it is almost always indirect.

why.A: Direct isn't controlled by deep-ring occlusion and rarely reaches the scrotum.
why.C: Spigelian is in the lateral abdominal wall.

stem: A 3 months old boy was seen in a pediatric surgery clinic and was diagnosed with right inguinal hernia. He was booked for elective herniotomy. Two weeks before his elective surgery he was presented to the pediatric emergency department with irritability and reluctant to feed. His mother noticed persistent right inguinal swelling for the last 3 hours. Which of the following is the best management option?

opts.t: Trial of hernia reduction under sedation and analgesia
Observation in emergency for spontaneous reduction

srcNote: (but be aware trial of hernia reduction is not an option if strangulated) (Common pediatric inguinoscrotal conditions tutorial)
expl: An incarcerated infant hernia without signs of strangulation → try reduction under sedation/analgesia (usually successful), then herniotomy after 24–48 h when oedema settles.

why.A: Emergency surgery if reduction fails or strangulation is suspected.

stem: A 6-month-old boy presented to the pediatric surgery clinic with absence of left testis since birth. On examination the left testis was not palpable in the left inguinal region and the right testis was normally located in the right he scrotum Which of the following is the best diagnostic modality for localizing the impalpable Testis?

opts.t: MRI scan of abdomen and pelvis.
CT scans of the abdomen and pelvis.

srcNote: d (Common pediatric surgical problems)
expl: For a truly non-palpable testis, diagnostic laparoscopy finds an intra-abdominal testis (or confirms absence) and allows treatment in the same sitting. Ultrasound can't reliably confirm a true testis.

why.A: Unreliable — may show nonspecific structures.
why.B: Poor sensitivity for small intra-abdominal testes, and needs sedation.

stem: Mother comes with child to general pediatric clinic with the complaint that when the child cries a bulge is apparent, on physical exam nothing was noted and there was bilateral descended testes. What will you do next?
srcNote: (Common pediatric surgical problems)
expl: A convincing history of a bulge on crying means an inguinal hernia even if nothing is found on examination; hernias never resolve → refer to paediatric surgery.

why.A: Imaging isn't needed — the history is enough.
why.C: Reassurance misses a hernia that risks incarceration.

stem: Child presenting with inguinal hernia. What is the characteristic that differentiate it from emergency cases?
srcNote: (Abdominal wall and herniae) Only three answer choices are supplied in the source.
expl: Reducibility separates an elective hernia from an emergency (incarcerated/strangulated).

why.A: Skin changes are a late sign.

stem: A 6 months old boy presented with his mother noticing a peri-anal red swelling for 2 days. On examination an 8 mm tender red swelling was noticed Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

opts.t: Warm water baths daily and re-evaluate after 7 days.
Incision and drainage with antibiotics for 5-7 days.

srcNote: (anorectal disease)
expl: A tender red perianal swelling in an infant = perianal abscess → incision and drainage; antibiotics are added in infants/cellulitis.

why.A: Delays drainage.
why.C: Antibiotics alone don't treat an abscess.

stem: A 2 month old child with bilateral hernia and hydrocele what is the best Management?

opts.t: Bilateral hernia repair and evacuation of the hydrocele.
Bilateral hernia repair and observe hydrocele.
Observe until two years of age.

srcNote: (not sure ) (Common pediatric surgical problems) The source marks its answer as uncertain; the original key is retained.
expl: Bilateral hernias with hydrocele (both from a patent processus vaginalis) → repair both hernias and deal with the hydrocele at the same operation.

why.A: Correct.
why.B: The hydrocele is evacuated at the same time.

stem: A 3 months old boy was seen in pediatric surgery clinic and was diagnosed as right inguinal hernia. He was booked for elective herniotomy. Two weeks before his elective surgery he has presented to pediatric emergency department with irritability and reluctant to feed. His mother noticed persistent of right inguinal swelling for the last 3 hours. Which of the following is the best management option?

opts.t: Trial of hernia reduction under sedation and analgesia
Observation in emergency for spontaneous reduction

srcNote: (Common pediatric surgical problems) Other source key (Final Year not stated Q33 (p. 264)): A. Reduction under anesthesia and sedation.. Answer: a (Common pediatric surgical problems) (Abdominal wall and herniae)
expl: An incarcerated infant hernia without signs of strangulation → trial of reduction under sedation and analgesia; if it reduces, keep the child admitted and do the herniotomy at the next available slot; if not, operate immediately.

why.A: Emergency surgery only if reduction fails or strangulation is suspected.

stem: Regarding undescended testis?

opts.t: orchiopexy is best done at 6-12 months
Laparoscopy is not valuable in management
The risk of torsion is less than normal testis
Patent ductus vaginalis almost never present in these patients.

expl: Orchidopexy is best done at 6–12 months.

why.A: Correct.
why.B: Malignancy risk is raised (several-fold) but nowhere near 20%.
why.C: Laparoscopy is the key tool for the impalpable testis — diagnostic and therapeutic.
why.D: Torsion risk is higher, not lower.
why.E: A patent processus vaginalis is present in most undescended testes.

stem: A newborn has a soft swelling in the neck, present at birth, in the posterior triangle, that transilluminates. What is the diagnosis?
srcNote: Cystic Hygroma :) Incomplete source recall; no answer choices are supplied.
ansText: Cystic hygroma (macrocystic lymphatic malformation) — present at birth, posterior triangle, soft and brilliantly transilluminant.
